subtitle: When people push back on equity work, start by examining the concern behind it. You will keep actual responsibilities in place and make the next step in the work practical.
scope: For leaders and supervisors across DHS. This course examines work responses to equity-related change; it does not diagnose employees, determine an IDI orientation, decide a misconduct case or authorize exceptions to required duties. Use practice material here and approved channels for actual information. Staff perform their own work with consultant guidance when useful. Excluded Native American or Tribal-specific matters go to the person or area responsible within ADSA (Aging and Disability Services Administration).
introTranscript: The word resistance can describe many different things, from a genuine workload barrier to an unsupported claim that needs to be challenged. Treating every question as resistance can hide useful information; treating every objection as a reason to stop can leave a required responsibility undone. Leaders need a more careful response. In this course you will examine what a concern actually says, distinguish information and practical barriers from a disagreement over methods, clarify required responsibilities and develop a bounded next action. You will also practice addressing stereotypes or formal concerns through their proper routes and reviewing whether a work change became useful. The aim is a stronger equity-work process, not a ranking of employees or an assumption about their motives. Different views can inform decisions without replacing the evidence, authority or follow-through the work requires.

lessons.title: Ask what the concern actually says
lessons.summary: Separate a work observation, a proposed explanation and an unsupported personal label.
lessons.objective: Describe a practice objection without assuming its speaker’s motive.
objectives: Describe a practice objection without assuming its speaker’s motive.
Distinguish a practical concern from an identity-based generalization.
Write a neutral question that reveals what needs examination.
takeaways: Resistance is a label, not a complete explanation.
Take a relevant concern seriously without accepting every claim.
Ask a specific work question before choosing the response.
lessons.statement: A careful first question can reveal the work issue that a broad label would hide.

image.caption: A useful response begins by understanding the specific question being raised.

intro.heading: What is the person asking you to examine?
intro.body:
A team is preparing an equity review of a proposed service change. One employee says the schedule does not allow the necessary evidence gathering. The leader calls that resistance and moves on. Another employee says a whole community will never use the service anyway. The leader accepts that statement as another legitimate concern. Both responses miss an important distinction. A practical schedule issue deserves examination, while a group generalization cannot substitute for evidence. The word resistance does not tell the leader which response is needed.

Describe the statement or behavior before explaining it. “The employee asked how research time would be allocated” is an observation. “They do not care about equity” is an interpretation that the observation does not establish. Someone may need information, disagree with the proposed method, face a practical barrier, question a decision or avoid a legitimate work responsibility. More than one issue may be present. A specific question helps identify the parts without diagnosing the person.

Use a neutral work prompt: “Which step concerns you, what information supports the concern and what would make that step workable?” This invites reasons and conditions. It does not require a private identity account or a loyalty statement. If the concern is based on a stereotype, name that limit and ask for relevant evidence instead. Respectful inquiry means examining a claim carefully, not giving every expressed explanation equal credibility.

The leader also needs to consider their own arrangement. The task may be unclear, the requested input may arrive after the decision or the support may not match the expectation. An employee’s question can expose a design problem rather than a personal failure. That possibility should not remove accountability to actual assigned work and policy. It should improve the explanation and conditions under which staff carry out their responsibilities.

Keep the inquiry proportionate. A course response or meeting objection cannot determine an individual IDI orientation, employment commitment or psychological state. Use practice information in this practice. For an actual concern, follow appropriate records and responsible guidance. Begin by understanding the work issue, then choose a response connected to evidence, authority and the next action.

lessons.keyStatement: Replace the broad label with a specific question about the work and evidence.

flashcards.back: A question, objection or account that needs its actual content examined.
A condition that makes a work step difficult to perform, such as unavailable time, access or support.
A proposed explanation for a statement or pattern; it is not established merely by being plausible.
An actual duty established by the applicable authority, distinct from a leader’s preferred method.
A way to carry out work; some aspects may be open to improvement while required duties remain.
A specific step with an owner, authority and suitable result check.

items.title: A schedule question
items.body: A request for workable research time can identify a real dependency. Ask which step needs time and what the decision schedule requires. Do not promise unlimited resources or assume the employee refuses the purpose. The leader can examine workload and sequencing while retaining responsibility for the required analysis and seeking authority for necessary changes.

items.title: A method disagreement
items.body: An employee may support the purpose while questioning whether a proposed meeting or form obtains useful evidence. Ask for the reasoning and alternatives. A preference is not automatically decisive, but may reveal a better approach. Compare options within actual constraints rather than requiring agreement with the leader’s first method as proof of commitment.

items.title: A group generalization
items.body: A claim that an entire community does not care about a service is not evidence of individual experience. Name the unsupported scope and return to appropriate information and perspectives. Do not ask a colleague to represent or defend the group. A conduct or formal concern may also require its responsible route, separate from the analytical question.

tabs.label: Apply a label
tabs.body: Calling the person resistant can feel efficient but leaves the cause unexamined. It may conceal a schedule, clarity or access gap the leader can address. The label also does not establish that an objection is reasonable. Return to what was actually said and ask for the relevant work evidence before deciding what response is warranted.

tabs.label: Accept every objection
tabs.body: Taking a concern seriously is different from adopting its explanation or stopping the work. A stereotype or unsupported claim should be challenged, and actual responsibilities remain. Examine reasons and conditions so the group can improve methods where appropriate without making objection alone a veto over a legitimate duty.

tabs.label: Ask a work question
tabs.body: A specific question identifies the step, evidence and practical condition at issue. This can distinguish a useful constraint from a misconception or unsupported generalization. The response may be clarification, support, method review or a formal route. None requires a personal cultural-development diagnosis or a loyalty test.

check.question: An employee asks how evidence-gathering time will fit the schedule. What is the strongest first response?
check.correct: Clarify the step, required work and practical dependency before assuming motive or deciding the response.
wrong: Label the employee resistant because questions slow the meeting.
Drop every equity responsibility as soon as anyone objects.
Infer the employee’s IDI orientation from the question.
check.feedbackCorrect: The leader can examine a practical condition while retaining actual responsibilities and appropriate boundaries.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The question alone does not establish resistance or motive. Objection does not erase required duties. A meeting statement cannot supply an assessed individual IDI orientation. Identify the actual step, evidence and dependency so the next response fits the work.

items.text: An employee asks how much research time is available.
A team member says the proposed form duplicates another approved step.
Does the schedule provide time for the required evidence?
Would another authorized method answer the same question better?
Anyone who asks a question lacks commitment to equity.
The objection proves the person’s assessed cultural-development orientation.

lessons.next: Next, distinguish different barriers so the response fits the actual concern.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Leader Asha schedules a service-change equity review. Staff member Ben asks who will gather missing evidence and when. Asha wants to record him as resistant. Another participant makes an unsupported claim about a whole racial community. The team needs both workable preparation and sound evidence; Asha cannot infer motives or personal assessments from the meeting.
scenario.prompt: Which response best improves the work?
options: Ask Ben about the actual evidence dependency, challenge the unsupported group claim and clarify next responsibilities.
Assign both speakers the same resistance score.
Cancel the review because the discussion was not immediately agreeable.
responses: This distinguishes useful inquiry from unsupported reasoning while retaining the work purpose.
The score hides different issues and creates an unjustified personal judgment.
Disagreement may identify work that needs attention; it does not itself remove the review responsibility.

lessons.transfer: Write a neutral question about an invented objection that identifies the step, evidence and condition needing examination.

move.control: You can examine the actual concern before choosing a response.
move.failure: A practical issue is silenced or an unsupported claim is accepted because both are called resistance.
move.next: In the next relevant discussion, separate the statement from the explanation you initially supplied.

lessons.title: Match the response to the barrier
lessons.summary: Distinguish unclear information, unavailable conditions and disagreement about a method.
lessons.objective: Classify the work issue in a practice concern without diagnosing a person.
objectives: Classify the work issue in a practice concern without diagnosing a person.
Choose a clarification or support action tied to the identified barrier.
Identify when more than one response is needed.
takeaways: More explanation will not fix every practical dependency.
Resources alone will not resolve an unclear purpose.
Several concerns can appear in the same statement.
lessons.statement: A response is more useful when it addresses the condition that actually prevents or weakens the work.

image.caption: Different work barriers require different questions and practical responses.

intro.heading: Is the next step unclear, unavailable or disputed?
intro.body:
A team member says, “This equity review will not work.” The statement may sound final, but its parts need examination. They may not understand the purpose, lack access to the approved information, have no time within the assigned workload or believe the proposed discussion method misses an important perspective. Repeating the same enthusiastic explanation will not necessarily address these different issues. Ask the person to identify the work step and reason, then examine what response fits.

An information gap concerns what the person needs to understand. The task may use an unexplained acronym, omit the decision question or leave authority unclear. Clarify the purpose, expected product and review route. Do not mistake a question about an unfamiliar method for a rejection of equity. A clear example or practice can help someone understand what they are expected to do without replacing their responsibility to perform the actual work.

A practical dependency concerns what is needed to carry out the step. Time, approved data access, a person to check the work or an appropriate accommodation may be unavailable. Confirm the dependency with responsible roles and address it through the applicable process. Do not tell staff to obtain private information through an unauthorized channel or work outside approved arrangements to demonstrate commitment. A leader must examine the conditions attached to the expectation.

A method disagreement concerns how to answer the work question. The employee may propose a different way to seek perspectives or compare options. Ask whether it addresses the purpose and actual requirements, what tradeoffs it creates and what evidence could distinguish it from the current method. The preferred option is not automatically the employee’s or the leader’s. Responsible comparison preserves the duty while improving the approach when evidence supports it.

Keep the boundaries practical rather than personal. These categories describe the work issue, not types of employees. The same person can raise several concerns or change their view after clarification. If a formal concern or stereotype arises, handle that part through the appropriate route. Do not replace it with more training merely because the conversation began as learning.

inThisLesson: Respond to more than one part.
lessons.keyStatement: Clarify, support or compare methods according to the issue, not a personal resistance category.

items.title: More messaging for an access gap
items.body: A reminder may communicate the deadline but cannot create approved data access. Confirm the missing dependency, its owner and a legitimate fallback. Avoid telling staff to borrow accounts or collect private records informally. The task still needs a responsible plan rather than either unsupported completion claims or abandoning the purpose.

items.title: More resources for a purpose gap
items.body: Providing extra time may not help when the employee does not understand the question. Explain the decision, expected contribution and why the evidence matters. A bounded example can reveal the next step. Check understanding through the work rather than a confidence rating, and keep the employee responsible for applying the explanation.

items.title: More persuasion for a method question
items.body: An alternative proposal needs comparison, not a loyalty contest. Ask how each option answers the question, whose perspectives it reaches and what constraints apply. The result may support the current approach or a revision. A leader can retain authority while examining criticism of their chosen method honestly.

tabs.label: Clarify
tabs.body: Clarification explains purpose, task and expected evidence. It is useful when the person cannot see what the review requires or how the result will be used. A worked practice example may help. It cannot supply unavailable access or make a formal concern disappear, so check whether understanding is the actual issue before repeating the explanation.

tabs.label: Support
tabs.body: Support addresses an identified practical dependency through responsible arrangements. Confirm who will check the work, authorized time or access path and check whether it works. Support does not mean promising unlimited resources or doing the entire analysis for staff. The person should be able to carry out the work with a usable arrangement and clear responsibility.

tabs.label: Compare
tabs.body: Comparison examines alternatives against the purpose and requirements. A smaller discussion may reach a missing perspective better, or may introduce another limit. State the evidence and tradeoffs rather than choosing from enthusiasm or status. An alternative can be promising without yet being authorized, and a required duty remains while its method is examined.

check.question: A team understands the review purpose but cannot access the approved evidence needed. What response fits?
check.correct: Confirm the dependency with the responsible role, arrange a legitimate access path or fallback and revise the work plan as authorized.
wrong: Repeat the purpose more loudly until access is no longer mentioned.
Ask staff to use a colleague’s account to prove commitment.
Take over every analysis permanently so staff never need the evidence.
check.feedbackCorrect: This addresses the practical condition while preserving approved access and staff responsibility.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Repeating purpose does not provide the missing evidence route. Borrowed accounts can bypass approved access and accountability. Permanent substitution prevents staff from developing and exercising capability. Confirm the dependency and responsible arrangement, then check whether the work can proceed legitimately.

items.text: The employee cannot tell which decision the review informs.
The expected analysis product has not been explained.
Required evidence is available only through an approved role not yet contacted.
The assigned schedule contains no agreed review time.
A proposed smaller discussion may reach a missing perspective.
The team questions whether two forms ask the same approved question.

lessons.next: Next, distinguish actual requirements from open choices in the method.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Supervisor Owen’s team understands why a notice needs review. The evidence contact is unavailable and no fallback is named. Colleague Imani also suggests an alternative discussion format that might reveal a missing perspective. Owen proposes sending another motivational email and asking the consultant to perform every analysis. Current access and decision requirements still apply.
scenario.prompt: Which response fits the identified issues?
options: Treat both concerns as proof of low commitment.
Confirm an approved evidence fallback and separately compare the proposed format with the work purpose and constraints.
Tell the team to gather unrestricted private records and use any format they prefer.
responses: The label loses the practical dependency and the method question.
This gives each issue a suitable response without bypassing authority or replacing staff work.
Improvement cannot authorize private-information collection or waive actual requirements.

lessons.transfer: Use an invented task to identify one information gap, one dependency and one method question, with a distinct next response for each.

move.control: You can diagnose the work arrangement without diagnosing the employee.
move.failure: The leader offers persuasion when a dependency needs repair or resources when the task needs clarification.
move.next: When a broad objection appears, ask which part needs clarification, support or comparison.

lessons.title: Keep requirements clear and methods open where appropriate
lessons.summary: Explain the actual duty, authority and choices without inventing exemptions or presenting a preference as policy.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a required work responsibility from a proposed learning method.
objectives: Distinguish a required work responsibility from a proposed learning method.
Identify who can authorize a method change or resolve a policy question.
Write a response that preserves accountability while inviting relevant improvement.
takeaways: Actual duties do not disappear because a method is questioned.
A preferred local approach is not automatically a policy requirement.
Explain authority before promising exceptions or outcomes.
lessons.statement: Clarity about what is required creates more useful room to improve what is genuinely open.

image.caption: A clear boundary separates the actual duty from choices about carrying it out.

intro.heading: What must happen, and what can improve?
intro.body:
A leader introduces an equity review and tells staff that a particular course and discussion format that are not required are mandatory policy requirements. The leader may want a consistent approach, but accuracy matters. A formal duty must be grounded in its actual authority. A learning activity or preferred local method that is not required should not be presented as policy merely because it supports the same purpose. Staff need to know which responsibilities apply, what is proposed and who decides questions about the process.

DHS equity policy establishes responsibilities for considering equity in work and using the appropriate formal analysis route where required. This course does not replace that policy, approve a new tool or decide that a particular proposal is exempt. Use the published policy and responsible agency guidance for actual work. A question about a method can prompt clarification or review without suspending a required responsibility simply because the group has not yet agreed on an approach.

Describe three things: the duty, the authorized decision and the open method choice. For example, a team may have a required analysis to perform, a responsible review of the proposed approach and some flexibility in how it organizes preparation within approved conditions. Do not promise flexibility the team lacks. A deadline, information rule or approved tool requirement may need another role’s decision. Name that dependency rather than treating a lively meeting as authorization.

Accountability should be understandable. Explain the task, expected evidence, responsible roles and work arrangements. Staff should be able to ask how to do it without being required to express agreement with every interpretation or share private experiences. Respectful disagreement is not the same as refusing assigned work. Likewise, a learning choice does not remove legitimate employment or policy responsibilities. Handle an actual work-performance question through responsible procedures, not an informal resistance score.

Where a method is open, examine alternatives seriously. A suggestion may simplify duplication or improve access to a perspective while retaining the required analysis. Compare its effect and limits, obtain needed authority and give a reasoned response. This strengthens the work rather than turning the choice into a contest between compliance language and unlimited discretion.

inThisLesson: Separate learning that is not required from work duty.
lessons.keyStatement: Do not invent a requirement or an exemption; clarify the real duty and decision route.

items.title: “My preference is the policy”
items.body: A leader can propose a useful method without claiming it is a published requirement. State its purpose and actual decision status, and check questions through responsible guidance. Inaccurate authority can discourage useful inquiry and make staff unsure which duties truly apply. A better explanation distinguishes policy, approved instructions and learning that is not required.

items.title: “Disagreement makes the work optional”
items.body: Questioning a format does not automatically remove the duty it supports. Clarify the concern and identify a workable authorized approach. Actual performance expectations remain with their proper procedures. The response should preserve both inquiry and accountability rather than using either a blanket exemption or a personal commitment label.

items.title: “The meeting can authorize everything”
items.body: Group support does not settle a data-use rule, tool approval or policy exception. Identify the role with authority and the question needing review. A proposed improvement can be recorded and developed while its decision remains open. Do not promise implementation before the responsible requirement has been checked.

tabs.label: Duty
tabs.body: A duty comes from the applicable authority and its actual scope. Explain it through current references and responsible guidance, not a slogan or a course title. Staff may need clarification to perform it well. A method objection should prompt a suitable response, while the duty continues through a legitimate work plan rather than disappearing by default.

tabs.label: Authority
tabs.body: Authority identifies who may decide a proposed change, exemption or formal question. The facilitator or consultant can provide guidance without assuming powers that belong elsewhere. If the role is unclear, seek clarification before promising a result. A majority in the room cannot confer control over policy, personnel or restricted information.

tabs.label: Open approach
tabs.body: An open approach is a genuine choice within approved constraints. The team might improve preparation, sequencing or a communication method without changing the required analysis. Compare options for usefulness and obtain needed authorization. Accurate flexibility can make work better; invented flexibility creates a promise the team cannot honor.

check.question: A leader calls a course that is not required the required policy analysis and offers to waive the real analysis if everyone attends. What should change?
check.correct: Explain that the course is not a requirement and preserve the actual required analysis and responsible review route.
wrong: Attendance should automatically replace every policy duty.
A leader’s verbal promise creates an exemption regardless of authority.
Staff should stop asking about methods because any question is refusal.
check.feedbackCorrect: This keeps learning, duty and authority distinct while allowing useful questions about how the work is performed.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Course attendance does not automatically fulfill the required analysis. A promise cannot create exemption authority. Treating every method question as refusal silences clarification without improving performance. Identify the actual duty and responsible process, then examine genuine open choices.

items.text: Use the applicable required equity-analysis process for covered work.
Obtain responsible guidance on whether a proposed method is authorized.
Practice with a practice example in this course.
Seek consultant feedback while retaining ownership of the analysis.
A meeting vote waives all data restrictions.
Attendance replaces the formal analysis because the topics overlap.

lessons.next: Next, make a bounded improvement that tests a method without testing whether rights or duties apply.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Leader Mae introduces a new practice exercise that is not required. She says completion replaces the formal equity review of a service proposal and that the team can vote to waive any evidence rule. Staff member Noel asks which authority applies. The consultant can help clarify the analytical question but cannot approve a waiver of unrelated requirements.
options: Keep the claim to avoid confusing staff with distinctions.
Rate Noel’s question as resistance and proceed.
Clarify that the exercise is not required, retain actual review requirements and seek responsible guidance about any proposed method change.
responses: A simpler inaccurate explanation still misstates authority and duty.
The question seeks necessary process information; a label does not answer it.
This repairs the authority claim and leaves room for legitimate method improvement.

lessons.transfer: For an invented task, write the duty, the responsible authority and one genuinely open method choice separately.

move.control: You can explain requirements accurately and avoid promises outside your authority.
move.failure: Learning that is not required becomes a false mandate or a method debate becomes an unauthorized exemption.
move.next: Before setting the next expectation, state which authority establishes it and which choices remain open.

lessons.title: Develop a bounded improvement and check its usefulness
lessons.summary: Turn a supported concern into a practical method change with an owner, support and appropriate evidence.
lessons.objective: Connect a proposed improvement to the barrier it addresses.
objectives: Connect a proposed improvement to the barrier it addresses.
Describe the action, support and authority for a practice method test.
Choose a check of usefulness that does not infer employee motives.
takeaways: A method test should examine the work, not people’s loyalty.
A small change needs clear scope and usable support.
Learning from a test does not authorize bypassing required procedures.
lessons.statement: A manageable improvement can reveal whether an approach helps while leaving actual rights, duties and decision authority intact.

image.caption: A practical improvement has a clear work purpose and a suitable result check.

intro.heading: What can the team try responsibly?
intro.body:
The team identifies duplication in an internal preparation step. One form asks staff to repeat evidence already documented in the approved review record. The leader wants to test a clearer reference instruction. This can be a useful bounded improvement if the responsible process permits it. The purpose is to see whether the instruction reduces confusion while preserving the needed analysis and record. It is not a trial of whether equity duties or participant rights should apply.

Begin with the supported barrier. Describe the observed duplication and its effect rather than declaring staff resistant to paperwork. Identify the proposed change and what it is intended to preserve. A simpler instruction may reduce unnecessary repetition but still need sufficient context for the reader to understand the evidence. Compare that tradeoff before presenting simplification as an automatic improvement.

Confirm the scope and authority. The leader may be able to clarify a local instruction but need approval to change a formal form or record requirement. Ask the responsible role and keep the decision visible. Use appropriate practice or non-identifying practice material when testing a learning method. Actual service or personnel information needs its authorized handling, and a test cannot waive restrictions merely because it is small.

Plan support. Name who performs the step, who checks the result and what time, information or access is needed. Staff should carry out their own work with suitable feedback. If the consultant supplies every completed analysis, the test will not show whether staff can use the new instruction. A bounded demonstration may help, followed by a chance for staff to apply the reasoning themselves.

Choose evidence tied to use. Ask whether the reader can locate and understand the relevant reasoning, whether staff can complete the step and what uncertainty remains. Count delivery separately from effect. A small exercise may justify refining an instruction without proving that every team will benefit or that a broader disparity has changed. If the improvement fails, examine the method and conditions rather than assigning negative personal labels to participants.

lessons.keyStatement: Test an authorized method change against its work purpose, not a personal commitment score.

items.title: The proposed change is only easier
items.body: Ease can matter, but the revised method must still answer the work question and preserve required evidence. Compare what would be removed and what the reader still needs. A shorter form may be an improvement or may hide reasoning. Check the task result rather than treating brevity alone as proof of usefulness.

items.title: The test has no support
items.body: A new instruction can fail because the contact, time or access is missing. Confirm those conditions before interpreting the outcome. The leader should not use unsupported difficulty as evidence that staff oppose equity. A test becomes more informative when participants have a legitimate opportunity to use the approach and describe the practical result.

items.title: The consultant supplies the result
items.body: Consultant guidance can explain the reasoning or offer a bounded example. It should not substitute every participant’s work and then be counted as staff capability. Give staff a chance to apply the method, receive feedback and revise. The purpose is usable independent practice with support, not dependence on one person’s finished output.

tabs.label: Delivery
tabs.body: Delivery shows that the instruction, material or arrangement was provided. It is a necessary part of the plan but not sufficient evidence of usefulness. A new form can be distributed and remain confusing. Record delivery accurately, then examine whether the intended work can actually be completed through the responsible process.

tabs.label: Usefulness
tabs.body: Usefulness concerns the task the method should enable. Ask whether staff can link evidence to reasoning and whether the reader can follow it. A suitable example can reveal a remaining gap. The check needs appropriate scope and information handling; it is not an assessment of each person’s moral commitment or cultural-development orientation.

tabs.label: Transfer
tabs.body: Transfer asks whether the reasoning can be applied to a different appropriate work example. A successful practice exercise may support further practice without certifying every real-world result. Staff should explain their own choice with useful guidance available. Broader implementation still needs actual authority, context and evidence rather than automatic expansion from one small test.

check.question: A method exercise produces clear analyses only because the consultant writes every answer. What does this establish?
check.correct: The supplied examples may help instruction, but staff capability to use the method independently has not yet been demonstrated.
wrong: Staff independence is proven because the outputs are polished.
Every staff member who needed help lacks commitment to equity.
The work should become permanently consultant-owned to avoid further practice.
check.feedbackCorrect: The test must distinguish useful demonstration from evidence of staff performing and applying the reasoning.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Polished substituted work does not establish staff capability. Asking for help does not prove low commitment. Making the consultant the permanent owner defeats the purpose of developing staff capacity. Use a bounded demonstration, then let staff perform, explain and revise the work with suitable support.

items.text: Confirm whether a local instruction can be revised within authority.
Provide practice material and a named feedback contact.
Ask whether the reader can follow the evidence-to-recommendation reasoning.
Have staff apply the instruction to a second appropriate example.
An unclear first answer proves the employee opposes equity.
A polished consultant answer proves every staff member works independently.

lessons.next: Next, preserve accountability when the concern involves conduct or formal duties.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Supervisor Felix wants to clarify a duplicated preparation instruction. The responsible role permits a practice trial without changing the required review record. Felix asks the consultant to write all practice analyses and plans to call that proof of staff independence. Colleague Hana suggests that staff try a new example with time and feedback so the instruction itself can be examined.
scenario.prompt: Which plan produces more useful evidence?
options: Use a bounded demonstration, then let staff apply the authorized instruction themselves and check the reasoning and result.
Score anyone who asks a question as resistant.
Remove the required review record because the trial should be flexible.
responses: This separates demonstration from staff practice and tests the intended work under suitable conditions.
The score supplies a personal label rather than information about the method.
A learning trial does not authorize removing a required record.

lessons.transfer: Create an invented method test with a barrier, authorized action, support, owner and usefulness check.

move.control: You can connect a method improvement to a supported barrier and realistic test conditions.
move.failure: The team declares capability from supplied outputs or changes required procedures without authority.
move.next: For the next authorized improvement, check the intended task result as well as delivery.

lessons.title: Set clear boundaries without using retaliation or identity labels
lessons.summary: Distinguish legitimate accountability, unsupported group claims and formal concern handling.
lessons.objective: Write a work expectation without requiring personal agreement or disclosure.
objectives: Write a work expectation without requiring personal agreement or disclosure.
Choose an appropriate response to a protected-class allegation raised during change discussion.
Identify an unsupported penalty or cultural-development inference in a practice plan.
takeaways: Clear expectations can coexist with respectful questions.
A stereotype needs a conduct boundary and sound evidence.
Formal reporting and anti-retaliation responsibilities remain in place.
lessons.statement: The leader can preserve required work without making agreement, silence or an inferred identity label the measure of performance.

image.caption: Accountability stays clearer when it is tied to the work and responsible procedures.

intro.heading: What responsibility applies now?
intro.body:
A leader may become frustrated when an equity-work discussion takes longer than expected. They propose removing opportunities from staff who ask questions or giving high ratings only to those who publicly endorse the approach. That substitutes personal agreement for an explained work standard. Staff should understand what task they must perform, what evidence is expected and which support and review arrangements apply. A leader’s preferred view or method is not itself the measure of every person’s performance.

Legitimate accountability remains important. If assigned work is not completed, examine the actual expectation, conditions and evidence through responsible procedures. Asking a method question does not remove the task; needing clarification does not establish refusal. Avoid turning an informal course response into a separate personnel score or using an inferred intercultural-development orientation to explain performance. A learning exercise is not an authorized individual assessment.

Address stereotypes directly. If someone dismisses a whole community as uninterested or undeserving, name the unsupported generalization and return to the relevant work evidence. The colleague affected does not have to defend the community or teach the group before the leader acts. A conduct issue may also raise formal duties. A calm boundary is compatible with appropriate accountability and does not require a public humiliation ritual.

When a protected-class harassment or discrimination allegation or incident arises, MMB Policy 1436 requires covered managers and supervisors to immediately report it to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow current agency procedures. The change discussion cannot vote on whether reporting is allowed, require a confrontation first or keep the matter solely in course notes. Pause unnecessary detail, take it seriously and retain the proper information path.

Avoid retaliation and inappropriate pressure. Actual policy and law govern protected activity and legitimate work responsibilities. Do not condition fair support on withdrawing a concern, staying silent or endorsing the leader’s conclusion. At the same time, not every objection has the same legal status, and the course cannot adjudicate a real situation. Seek responsible guidance, preserve accurate records and keep actual employment decisions tied to their proper authority and evidence.

lessons.keyStatement: Tie accountability to the actual work, and handle protected concerns through their required route.

items.title: “Agree with me to earn an opportunity”
items.body: A leader can explain a required task without making personal endorsement a hidden selection criterion. Removing development access because someone asked a relevant question may suppress useful inquiry and requires responsible scrutiny. Use the actual applicable process and evidence for employment decisions rather than a loyalty test created during a meeting.

items.title: “Their IDI stage explains the objection”
items.body: A course answer or meeting statement cannot supply an assessed individual orientation. Such a label can bypass the task conditions and become an unsupported personnel judgment. Examine the actual concern and performance evidence. Intercultural learning supports better inquiry and adaptation; it does not authorize the leader to diagnose an employee from disagreement.

items.title: “Keep the allegation inside our discussion”
items.body: An informal change process cannot replace required concern handling. Covered managers retain immediate reporting duties under Policy 1436 when a protected-class allegation or incident arises. Explain the proper route and limit unnecessary shared detail. The team can retain a suitable general work question without investigating an individual matter by group vote.

tabs.label: Work expectation
tabs.body: Explain the actual task, relevant evidence and support. Staff can ask questions or disagree with a method while still being responsible for legitimate work. Review a performance issue through current procedures rather than a meeting-based commitment score. Accountability becomes more usable when the expectation is observable and the conditions are examined honestly.

tabs.label: Conduct boundary
tabs.body: A stereotype or personal attack can undermine participation and reasoning. Name the behavior or claim that must change without requiring the affected colleague to educate the group. Seek responsible guidance where needed. Setting a boundary does not mean announcing a legal outcome or diagnosing the speaker’s cultural-development orientation.

tabs.label: Formal handling
tabs.body: A protected-class allegation or incident carries the applicable reporting and process duties. For covered managers, Policy 1436 requires immediate reporting to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. Do not delay for an informal resolution or demand withdrawal to provide support. The actual authorized process determines handling and any finding.

check.question: A supervisor receives a protected-class discrimination allegation during a change discussion. What should happen?
check.correct: The supervisor should immediately report it to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer under Policy 1436 and follow current procedures, with appropriate information handling.
wrong: The team should vote on whether the concern deserves reporting.
The employee must first endorse the equity initiative to receive support.
The supervisor should infer an IDI orientation and use it as the case finding.
check.feedbackCorrect: The actual reporting responsibility continues regardless of the discussion’s original purpose.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A group vote cannot confer permission to postpone a duty. Support cannot be conditioned on endorsing the initiative. An inferred orientation is not a formal finding or justified assessment. Follow the reporting route, protect unnecessary shared details and keep any general process improvement separate.

items.text: Complete the assigned comparison using the approved evidence and review route.
Raise the blocked dependency before the agreed review point.
Immediately report a covered allegation through the required manager route.
Keep actual concern records in approved channels.
Only employees who publicly agree will receive development access.
Infer cultural-development orientations from who questioned the method.

lessons.next: Next, review whether the response improved the work without declaring motives or universal success.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Supervisor Leila faces questions about a review method. She considers removing a development opportunity from a staff member who asked about workload. Another employee raises a protected-class discrimination allegation. Leila proposes using an inferred IDI orientation to decide the allegation and keeping everything in the learning exercise so the initiative looks collaborative.
scenario.prompt: Which response preserves the actual responsibilities?
options: Use the orientation label because it creates a simple explanation.
Clarify the work expectation and conditions, avoid the unsupported penalty, and fulfill immediate reporting and current procedures for the allegation.
Ask the group to decide whether the employee is loyal enough to be heard.
responses: The inference is unsupported and cannot replace work evidence or case handling.
This separates accountability, support and formal concern handling while preserving legitimate work.
A loyalty test adds a barrier and cannot establish the appropriate process.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice expectation and a separate concern-handling response without using agreement, silence or personal development labels as proxies.

move.control: You can explain actual work and fulfill reporting duties without inventing a personal score.
move.failure: Questions lead to unsupported penalties or a learning discussion delays formal concern handling.
move.next: Before responding to a difficult exchange, identify the work, conduct and formal responsibilities separately.

lessons.title: Review progress with evidence and adjust the response
lessons.summary: Distinguish a delivered response from a useful work change and retain remaining questions.
lessons.objective: Interpret a practice response pattern without claiming a personal motive.
objectives: Interpret a practice response pattern without claiming a personal motive.
Separate delivery, usefulness and uncertainty in a progress account.
Choose a next improvement with an owner and authority boundary.
takeaways: Silence is not proof that the concern disappeared.
A delivered explanation or support step needs a usefulness check.
Review the arrangement and work evidence rather than ranking people.
lessons.statement: Progress is better demonstrated by clearer work and usable follow-through than by fewer questions in the room.

image.caption: A quiet meeting leaves questions about the work that evidence still needs to answer.

intro.heading: Did the response help the work?
intro.body:
After a leader clarifies a task and arranges evidence access, fewer questions appear in the next meeting. The leader wants to report that resistance has ended. That conclusion goes beyond the observation. Fewer questions may reflect clearer understanding, less opportunity to contribute, a changed workload or concern about being labeled. The leader cannot choose a motive from silence. Examine whether the work became more understandable and usable through appropriate evidence.

Separate delivery and effect. A task explanation was sent; an approved access contact was assigned; a method was revised. Those are delivered steps. A reader can follow staff reasoning, the team obtains needed evidence through the correct route or participants can use the revised instruction. Those are possible signs of usefulness within a defined scope. Neither automatically proves that every concern ended or that a broader disparity changed because of the initiative.

Keep unknowns visible. Missing input may warrant a suitable follow-up opportunity, not a reassuring dashboard symbol. Limited information should neither be exaggerated nor discarded automatically. Ask which question matters for the next decision and what authorized evidence could answer it. Avoid collecting personal identities from names, assigning developmental orientations or creating informal commitment scores to make the account seem complete.

Review the response itself. Did clarification address the actual information gap? Did the arranged support resolve the dependency? Did a revised method preserve the purpose and required process? A response can be well intentioned and still fail to fit the barrier. If it did not help, revise the arrangement or obtain responsible guidance rather than declaring the employee resistant to every possible solution.

Name the next owner and check. Staff remain responsible for the analysis and action appropriate to their roles; the consultant offers guidance and feedback. A formal concern still has its own route even when the work arrangement improves. Explain what will continue, what needs revision and what remains uncertain. The account should make progress visible without demanding a public agreement statement or universal success claim.

lessons.keyStatement: Review what the response enabled, not what silence supposedly says about people.

items.title: Fewer questions prove agreement
items.body: The count can describe meeting activity but cannot establish why it changed. Ask whether the task is clearer and whether suitable contribution routes remain usable. A leader who previously penalized questions should not treat quietness as endorsement. Evidence of understanding and work performance is more useful than an inferred motive.

items.title: The support was assigned, so the issue is solved
items.body: A named contact may still be unavailable or lack authority to provide the evidence. Confirm the appropriate arrangement and result. Delivery matters, but a usefulness check reveals whether the response addressed the dependency. If the barrier remains, revise the plan or seek responsible guidance rather than blaming the employee for repeating it.

items.title: The outcome changed, so one cause is proven
items.body: Several workplace or program conditions may change alongside an initiative. Describe the trend and relevant process evidence with limits. A positive result can support continued inquiry without proving sole causation. A disappointing result likewise does not automatically establish poor commitment; examine the method, conditions and appropriate next action.

tabs.label: What was done
tabs.body: Record the actual explanation, support or method change with owner and timing. Avoid combining promises and delivered actions. A clear record helps the team see where follow-through remains incomplete, without exposing private personnel information. It is a starting point for review, not automatic evidence that every intended effect occurred.

tabs.label: What was enabled
tabs.body: Describe the bounded result the work evidence supports, such as staff locating the approved information and explaining their comparison. Include the conditions and scope. Consultant-written answers do not establish staff independence, and attendance does not prove useful application. Look for the task the response was intended to make possible.

tabs.label: What remains
tabs.body: Name the unresolved dependency, missing perspective or outcome question and its responsible next route. Unknowns should not be replaced with reassurance or a personal label. Select a proportionate follow-up tied to a decision. Preserve formal concern handling separately and explain who performs the work with any guidance needed.

check.question: Questions fell after a supervisor labeled objectors resistant, but no work-usefulness check occurred. What is justified?
check.correct: Only the observed question pattern is established; the supervisor should examine whether participation and work understanding are usable rather than infer agreement or motive.
wrong: Silence proves everyone now supports the approach.
Nonparticipants should receive low commitment scores.
All equity barriers must have been removed because the meeting was shorter.
check.feedbackCorrect: The account retains the observation and directs inquiry to practical work and participation conditions.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Silence cannot establish endorsement. Nonparticipation cannot justify a personal commitment score. A shorter meeting does not prove equity barriers disappeared. Describe what occurred, examine the actual task and participation arrangements, and state what evidence remains needed for the next decision.

items.text: The supervisor sent the revised task explanation.
The approved evidence contact was named in the work plan.
Staff obtained the needed information through the proper route.
The reader could follow the staff-owned comparison reasoning.
No questions means all staff have the same interpretation.
A shorter meeting proves every barrier was removed.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to examine a concern and plan a bounded response.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Leader Mika clarified a review task and arranged an approved evidence contact. Questions decreased, but the contact remained unavailable and staff could not finish the comparison. Mika wants to celebrate the end of resistance. The consultant offers feedback on the plan; the team remains responsible for its work and the real dependency still needs a responsible owner.
scenario.prompt: Which account and action are strongest?
options: Declare agreement because the room became quiet.
Assign low commitment to everyone with an unfinished comparison.
Record the delivered steps and unresolved access, repair the dependency through the responsible role and check whether staff can perform the task.
responses: Quietness does not establish understanding, access or agreement.
The score skips the known dependency and creates a personal inference.
This keeps progress and limits visible while addressing the actual remaining barrier.

lessons.transfer: Write an invented progress account with delivery, usefulness, uncertainty and the next responsible action separately.

move.control: You can review the response’s fit and retain honest evidence limits.
move.failure: Silence becomes proof of agreement while the actual work barrier remains.
move.next: At the next review point, check whether the response enabled the intended task and revise it where necessary.

jobAid.subtitle: Examine a concern and choose the response that fits the work.
remember: Describe the statement before assigning a motive.
Distinguish information, dependencies and method questions.
Challenge stereotypes without making a colleague defend a whole community.
Keep actual duties and authority separate from personal learning.
Managers retain applicable immediate reporting responsibilities.
Check usefulness without personal resistance scores or inferred IDI results.

sections.heading: Understand the issue
items: What work step, observation or proposed explanation is being raised?
Which relevant evidence supports it, and what remains unknown?
Does it identify unclear information, a practical dependency or a method choice?
Does a stereotype or formal concern require a separate response?
Which neutral question would clarify the actual condition?

sections.heading: Plan the response
items: Explain the duty, responsible authority and genuinely open choices.
Address the barrier through approved information and work arrangements.
Let staff perform the work with suitable guidance rather than permanent substitution.
Define a bounded method test only where authorized.
Preserve formal reporting, private records and legitimate employment processes.

sections.heading: Review the result
items: Record delivered actions separately from promises.
Check whether the intended task became understandable and usable.
Keep missing responses and causal questions uncertain.
Retain actual concerns in their appropriate routes.
Name the next owner, authority and proportionate evidence check.
